title: Ofcom on STV changes: AI responses, licensing and regional news
label: 9 September 2026 · STV cuts hearing
summary: Ofcom explained why it approved STV’s plan to share much news production between its north and central licences, defended a delayed decision caused largely by a big wave of AI-assisted consultation replies, and argued it balanced audience trends, digital growth and the financial strain on broadcasters while keeping local reporting teams in place. Committee members pressed Ofcom on the consultation handling, whether public responses mattered, and the risks to rural audiences.

chapters.title: Who does what for Gaelic and regional broadcasting?
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says the system with MG ALBA, the BBC and the Scottish Government looks complicated but generally works: Ofcom oversees certain duties (like recommending MG ALBA board appointments and holding the Gaelic media fund) while funding and some policy choices sit with ministers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Let's start simple: can you introduce yourselves and explain who does what for Gaelic broadcasting? There seem to be a lot of organisations involved.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: I’m the director of Ofcom Scotland. Ofcom is the UK regulator for TV, radio and telecoms — we set and enforce rules and supervise services in Scotland.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I run broadcasting regulation at Ofcom. I spent 35 years in journalism before joining, so I care about news services.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the number of organisations involved in Gaelic broadcasting create governance problems? Could no-one own the long-term future?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: It can look complex: MG ALBA (the body that runs Gaelic broadcasting), the BBC, Ofcom and the Scottish Government all have roles. For us the duties are fairly narrow: we recommend MG ALBA board appointments to ministers, we hold the Gaelic media fund (that’s grant money from the Scottish Government that MG ALBA draws down), and we meet MG ALBA regularly on performance.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: There’s also an MOU — a working agreement — between the Scottish Government and MG ALBA. Ofcom doesn’t set that MOU; ministers do. So overall it’s shared, but it’s working in practice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about BBC ALBA and the BBC operating licence — is BBC ALBA properly visible in that framework?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: The BBC’s operating licence sets conditions like hours and spending for services, so those rules do cover BBC ALBA — for example there are provisions about hours and spend and how the BBC meets its public purposes. But BBC ALBA isn’t singled out with its own long report; Ofcom’s annual BBC report looks at the whole BBC against its public purposes.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We also publish other work — like Media Nations Scotland — with sections on Gaelic broadcasting, the Commonwealth Games coverage partnerships, Gaelic podcasting and spend and hours. So there’s more visibility outside the BBC annual report too.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: So if anyone wants to scrutinise the MOU between Scottish Government and MG ALBA, that’s more for Holyrood than for you?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Yes. Ofcom has statutory, ‘fiduciary’ duties we work within. Questions about the adequacy of funding or making Gaelic duties statutory sit with governments and parliaments.

chapters.title: Why the decision on STV was delayed (AI-assisted replies)
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom says the delay was because a large campaign used an AI-assisted tool that generated about 1,196 individual-style responses (around 90% of roughly 1,300 replies) containing personal data and prefilled text; Ofcom read each one and had to cleanse and analyse them, which took longer than planned.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: You were due to announce your STV decision before Easter but delayed until after the Scottish election. The NUJ called that 'astonishing' — why did you delay?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: It was a hard decision and we wanted to consider everything fully. We got a lot of consultation replies — unusually many were produced via an AI-assisted campaign tool — and we had to go through them carefully.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Timeline in short: STV first sent a case in mid-October, a revised one in late November, we published a consultation in mid-December that closed in mid-February, and we issued our final decision on 1 June. The campaign 'Save STV North' used a tool that generated about 1,196 AI-assisted emails — roughly 90% of just over 1,300 total responses. They looked like individual emails and included personal data, so we read every one and had to remove personal data before analysis.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: But elections are fixed. Why say 'before Easter' if you wouldn't publish during the formal election period?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We hoped to finish before Easter. We didn't anticipate that volume and format of AI-assisted responses and couldn't complete the cleansing and analysis in the time window before the formal election period when we typically avoid publications that could be political.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: With respect, 1,300 messages isn't many for public bodies used to campaigns. It sounds like Ofcom was caught on the hop by AI.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We weren't surprised people cared, but the novelty was the AI-assist format and the personal data attached. It was the way the responses were delivered that made handling them more complex.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: Did you publish every one of the roughly 1,300 responses, or did you treat them as a single batch? How many did you publish?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We read every individual response. I don't have the precise count of how many were published individually on the website today, but we will write to the Committee with the exact figures.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: If you checked them all, why not go back to people to ask if they wanted personal data removed or to confirm their views?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: The campaign tool generated emails from people without giving us the usual options to publish or suppress personal data. We didn't go back to every individual; instead we removed personal data ourselves and analysed the content.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: Shouldn't Ofcom have expected different digital methods and planned for them? It feels worrying you needed extra time for a predictable campaign.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: We're learning. Lots of public bodies face similar AI-assisted responses now. We're investing in tools to detect AI-generated or AI-assisted replies and to triage large numbers in future so we can stick to expected timelines.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: But did the AI-assisted nature change how you weighed the responses? Or was it just volume?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We treated them the same as other responses. It was mainly the volume and the data-cleaning burden that slowed the process, not that AI replies were considered worth less or more.

chapters.title: What Ofcom decided on STV and why
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom rejected STV’s original plan for completely shared news, required a revised 70:30 (central:north) split with retained journalists in local bases and a stronger digital strategy, and said it was balancing falling linear audiences, rising digital consumption, and STV’s financial pressures.

turns.speaker: Lillian Jones
turns.text: STV changed its plan before your decision. How big was the change?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: STV first proposed 100% shared content for north and central. We said that wouldn’t meet the licence rules on regional distinctiveness, so it reworked the plan and offered a 70:30 split — meaning about 30% bespoke content for the north on weekdays. We published both of STV’s submissions alongside the consultation.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: The original submission also lacked a digital news strategy. We insisted on clearer digital commitments and more bespoke regional content in the north than the first plan had.

turns.speaker: Susan Murray
turns.text: Is the new STV service weaker than before?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: I don’t think it's weaker — it's different. The production of the 6pm show is more shared, but the journalists doing local reporting remain in Aberdeen, Inverness and Dundee, and STV has increased regional digital news. Early digital figures are up: digital video views went from roughly 64 million a month to about 80 million.

turns.speaker: Douglas McAllister
turns.text: But most consultation replies were against the change. Did those views affect your decision?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We read every response and took sentiment into account, but decisions need evidence. Nobody produced new factual evidence that would alter the balance. Importantly, we didn’t accept STV’s first plan — we forced a better outcome than what was originally proposed.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Also remember the bigger picture: we’d already assessed in 2022 that the cost of regional news would likely be a net cost for STV and that has worsened. Our role includes judging whether a licence change still delivers regional distinctiveness in a sustainable way.

turns.speaker: Dave Doogan
turns.text: It looks like public consultation didn’t change the outcome. Why should people bother responding in future?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Consultations matter. In this case, responses shaped elements — for instance the written licence commitments that keep journalistic resource in the north. We used people’s views alongside audience figures, economic analysis and other evidence.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: STV’s licence was renewed for ten years from 1 January 2025. Months later it asked to change it. Does that open a precedent for others to renege?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Broadcasters can approach us at any time to vary licence terms if circumstances change. But we can only change licences within the legal framework and the decisions ministers previously took about Channel 3 provisions. We scrutinise each request carefully.

turns.speaker: Mr MacDonald
turns.text: I'm worried about centralisation hurting the Highlands. Has closure or staff loss in places like Inverness been approved?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: Ofcom didn't allow the closure of newsrooms. STV must keep journalistic resource in those locations; there were no compulsory redundancies that we required. Production shifted, but newsgathering teams remained on the ground to feed both TV and digital output.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: I watched recent north and central bulletins: some north-origin stories ran across both editions, which shows the news can still reflect regional issues while reaching more people.

chapters.title: Wider risks: audiences, sustainability and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Ofcom accepts risks for older or hard-to-reach audiences as news moves digital, will monitor impact, is exploring tech to handle AI in consultations, and says any future licence changes would face the same scrutiny and evidence tests.

turns.speaker: Maureen Burke
turns.text: Did you assess impact on different communities and older viewers who may not use digital services?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Yes — we do statutory impact assessments, and we flagged that older viewers in rural areas could be hit by less linear coverage. We balanced that against better broadband and rising digital consumption. We’ll keep monitoring to avoid leaving anyone behind.

turns.speaker: Douglas Lumsden
turns.text: STV spent money on other projects like a new radio station while cutting news — did you check for alternative savings?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: How STV spends its money is a commercial decision for STV. Our job is to make sure licence obligations — regional distinctiveness and journalistic resource — are met. We can’t dictate internal commercial choices.

turns.speaker: Kirsteen Sullivan
turns.text: Do you accept that many people feel this was an easy cut and that regional news is an obvious place to make savings?

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: There’s pressure across the public service media sector — ITV, Channel 4 and the BBC face big savings. We aim to protect public service outcomes while recognising financial realities. We wrote safeguards into the revised licence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: One last question: you said you expected consultees to bring new evidence if they wanted to change your decision. How does the public, typically, provide that kind of evidence opposing a broadcaster's own figures?

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We welcome evidence from anyone — ministers, councils, trade bodies and individuals. We don’t expect ordinary people to produce detailed financial models, but sometimes stakeholders surface factual points we haven’t seen. The First Minister's submission is just as relevant as a viewer’s — different contributors bring different kinds of evidence.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. We’ll expect your follow-up on exact publication counts of consultation replies and any further monitoring data.

turns.speaker: Cristina Nicolotti Squires
turns.text: We will write with the figures and we’ll continue reporting on STV’s performance. Thanks for the chance to explain a difficult decision.

turns.speaker: Glenn Preston
turns.text: Thank you. We’ll follow the impacts closely and share the data the Committee needs.
